newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government gets back to work after holiday.
newsitem.headline: French government gets back to work after holiday.

text.p: France's new leftist government, getting back to work after a three-week holiday, is expected to approve plans on Wednesday to create 350,000 jobs for young people and carry out a switch to an all-volunteer army.

The cabinet of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin meets for the first time since July 30, marking the first major government event of this year's "Rentree", the traditional return to work and school after the summer holiday break.
Trade union leaders have criticised Jospin, who came to power in June, for his go-slow approach to the problem of joblessness, which stands at a record 12.6 percent.
But government officials say the jobs bill to be proposed to the cabinet on Wednesday proves Jospin's commitment to his campaign promise to make employment his top priority.
The bill is intended to create 100,000 jobs during 1998 without driving up public deficits, Employment Ministry officials said on Tuesday.
The bill's estimated price-tag is 11.9 billion to 13.8 billion francs (($1.9 billion to 2.2 billion) in 1998, with 80 percent to be paid by the state.

But the state funds are to be diverted from other programmes and thus will not affect the government's pledge to meet the three per cent deficit target required for European economic and monetary union, the officials said.

The defence reform measure, part of a plan to phase out conscription in France, would require that all young people, including women, be called up for a single day before their 18th birthday to learn about defence issues.

The bill would scrap a controversial plan put forward by the previous centre-right government to call up young people for five days, in order to assess their suitability for the military and to lecture them on patriotism.

The five-day plan, the brainchild of former defence minister Charles Millon, was intended to keep a link between the armed forces and the public at large as France moves to an all-professional force by 2002.
Officials decided to keep a single-day programme at the request of the military, which saw it as a useful opportunity to interest youths in careers in the armed forces .
This year's Rentree promises to be particularly charged because Jospin, who came to power in June, had put off key decisions on Europe, spending, taxation and jobs.
He said he needed the time to determine the true condition of state finances inherited from the previous government.

Now the time has come for him to disclose how he plans to fulfil campaign pledges to hold down public deficits sufficiently to launch European monetary union while creating 700,000 new jobs, cutting the value added tax on basic goods and preserving fragile economic growth.
Wednesday's cabinet meeting might also trigger a debate with President Jacques Chirac, who has vowed to keep the French military strong despite a reduction in troop strength.

Chirac associates predict that the conservative Chirac, forced to share power with the left after calling a snap election in which he lost his centre-right majority in parliament, will warn Jospin against significant defence spending cuts in 1998.
Jospin is expected to seek major cuts in order to fund domestic needs and still meet the deficit target set for the launch of a single European currency. ($ = 6.182 French Francs)
